\chapter{Twenty, A Hundred, And A Price With A Figure In It}
\label{ch:mw-numbered-price}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can understand the amount a seller names and answer it with a figure of my own.}

The round amounts a stall names are taught, the price question of chapter 27 finally gets an answer, and an old verb takes a figure to become a counter-offer.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bīs]{Hear \emph{bīs} — twenty}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-hear-bees}



\begin{quote}
Recall the ten-number payoff, write the show request, then say ten.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{chār} and \emph{pāṅch}, two chapters back, and the \textbf{\mw{च}} they share
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{bīs} — \textbf{twenty}
\end{quote}

Long \emph{ī}, then the same closing \emph{s} as \emph{das}. Marwari marks its tens with that \emph{s}: \emph{das}, \emph{bīs}.

Twenty arrives before the numbers between ten and twenty, and that is not an accident of ordering. Marwari builds nineteen by subtraction — \emph{ughaṇīs}, one short of twenty — the same way the dictionary records \emph{ekuṇcālīs}, one short of forty, for thirty-nine. A language that counts down to its round numbers has to be taught the round number first. Teaching the teens before twenty would print twenty in bold in a lesson that had not taught it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bīs]{\mw{बीस} — twenty on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-bees}



\begin{quote}
Recall the four-skill show payoff, then write ten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ब}} + \textbf{\mw{ी}} + \textbf{\mw{स}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{बीस}} — \emph{bīs} — twenty
\end{quote}

Every piece is second-hand. \textbf{\mw{ब}} came in with \textbf{\mw{बस}}, the bus. \textbf{\mw{ी}} came in with \textbf{\mw{पाणी}}. \textbf{\mw{स}} closes \textbf{\mw{दस}} as well.

Write \textbf{\mw{दस}} and \textbf{\mw{बीस}} one under the other and look at the last sign of each.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{बीस}}, cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write \textbf{\mw{दस}} and \textbf{\mw{तीन}} beneath and mark the long \textbf{\mw{ी}} where it appears.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[so]{Hear \emph{so} — a hundred}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-hear-so}



\begin{quote}
Say how much, say twenty, then say nine.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{chha} and \emph{sāt}, two chapters back, and where each closes
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{so} — \textbf{a hundred}
\end{quote}

One consonant and one long vowel. The largest number this book teaches is the shortest word in it.

Say \emph{do}, \emph{no}, \emph{so}. Two, nine, a hundred: all three are one consonant plus the same long \emph{o}, and nothing but that consonant tells them apart. At a noisy counter this is where a price gets misheard, so it is worth drilling the three together rather than in the order they were taught.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[so]{\mw{सो} — a hundred on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-so}



\begin{quote}
Say how much, then write twenty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{स}} + \textbf{\mw{ो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{सो}} — \emph{so} — a hundred
\end{quote}

Now write the three short ones in a column: \textbf{\mw{दो}}, \textbf{\mw{नो}}, \textbf{\mw{सो}}. The mark on the right never changes. The letter on the left is the entire difference between two, nine and a hundred.

That column is worth keeping. It is the one place in this book where a single mistaken stroke changes a price by a factor of fifty.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{दो}}, \textbf{\mw{नो}}, \textbf{\mw{सो}} from dictation, given out of order, three times over. Then read your own column back and say each amount.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye kitṇe kū hai? — bīs.]{Hear the answer — \emph{bīs.}}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-hear-price-number}



\begin{quote}
Write how much, then say a hundred and twenty.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{āṭh} and \emph{no}, two chapters back, and which of the two opens on a standing vowel
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ye kitṇe kū hai?} — \textbf{how much is this?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bīs.} — \textbf{twenty.}
\end{quote}

Chapter 27 taught the question. The answer had no words in it, so a learner who asked got a sound back and nothing else.

The answer turn is one word long. A seller names the figure and stops; there is no verb, no unit, no sentence. That is what makes it hearable — the whole of it is a number, and this book now has twelve of them.

Hear the same question answered \emph{das}, \emph{bīs}, \emph{so} in turn and say which is dearest.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye kitṇe kū hai? — bīs.]{\mw{ये} \mw{कितणे} \mw{कू} \mw{है}? — \mw{बीस।}}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-price-number}



\begin{quote}
Say the price question, then write ten and a hundred.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ये} \mw{कितणे} \mw{कू} \mw{है}?} — \textbf{\mw{बीस।}}
\end{quote}

The question was writable in chapter 27. The answer became writable two lessons ago. Putting them on one line adds no sign at all.

Note the danda after the answer. A price is a complete turn even at one word long, and Devanagari closes it the same way it closes a sentence.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write the question and answer as two lines. Then rewrite the answer line three times with \textbf{\mw{दस}}, \textbf{\mw{बीस}} and \textbf{\mw{सो}} in turn, and read each pair aloud.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das karo.]{Hear \emph{das karo} — make it ten}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-hear-counter-offer}



\begin{quote}
Write the price question, say make it, then say five.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{das}, and the two bare consonants it is written with
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{das karo.} — \textbf{make it ten.}
\end{quote}

Chapter 28 taught \emph{thoṛu sasto karo} — make it a bit cheaper. That is a wish. It names no figure, so the seller decides what a bit means.

Put a number where \emph{thoṛu sasto} stood and the same verb becomes an offer. The buyer names the price now.

Hear the pair run end to end: the seller says \emph{bīs}, the buyer says \emph{das karo}. This is the first exchange in the book where both sides have said an amount.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das karo.]{\mw{दस} \mw{करो।} — make it ten}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-counter-offer}



\begin{quote}
Write the price answer, then write twenty on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{दस}} + \textbf{\mw{करो।}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{दस} \mw{करो।}} — \emph{das karo.} — make it ten
\end{quote}

Nothing new for the hand. \textbf{\mw{करो}} came in with the bargaining request, \textbf{\mw{दस}} came in two chapters ago, and the number goes in front.

Swap the figure and the offer changes: \textbf{\mw{पांच} \mw{करो।}}, \textbf{\mw{बीस} \mw{करो।}}. The verb never moves.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{दस} \mw{करो।}} from a cover. Then write the same line twice more with \textbf{\mw{पांच}} and \textbf{\mw{बीस}} in the number slot, and read all three aloud as offers against a seller's \textbf{\mw{सो।}}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The three round amounts}

\label{lesson:MW-R34-round-recall}



\begin{quote}
Ask how much altogether, hear twenty, and offer ten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Hear \textbf{\mw{दस}}, \textbf{\mw{बीस}}, \textbf{\mw{सो}} in any order and say each.
  \item Say which two share a closing sign, and which two share a vowel mark.
  \item Write the three-way column \textbf{\mw{दो}}, \textbf{\mw{नो}}, \textbf{\mw{सो}} and read it back.
  \item Write \textbf{\mw{दस}}, \textbf{\mw{बीस}}, \textbf{\mw{सो}} from dictation, given out of order.
\end{enumerate}

Then run four counter-offers: hear a price, halve it, and say the offer.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — a price, understood and answered}

\label{lesson:MW-C34-numbered-price}



\begin{quote}
Write the total question and the make-it word, then recall the ten-number payoff.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Three turns, scored in four skills.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Listening.} Hear the price question answered with a figure, ten times over with different figures, and write each amount down.
  \item \textbf{Speaking.} Ask the price, hear a figure, and answer with a counter-offer that names a lower one.
  \item \textbf{Reading.} Read six printed exchanges and say, for each, what the seller asked and what the buyer offered.
  \item \textbf{Writing.} Write a whole three-turn exchange from dictation, with no model.
\end{enumerate}

Pass each separately.

This is what the numbers were for. Chapters 26 to 31 built a five-turn counter exchange in which the buyer could ask a price four different ways and understand no answer to any of them. The turn that was missing was one word long.

Still untaught: any figure between ten and twenty, and any way of refusing an offer and walking away.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Close the writing loop for \mw{ब}, \mw{स} and \mw{ो}}

\label{lesson:MW-R34-script-close}



\begin{quote}
Recall the numbered-price payoff, then recall the four-skill price payoff from chapter 27 and say what the second one could not do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write two single signs and one mark from sound cues: \textbf{\mw{ब}}, \textbf{\mw{स}}, \textbf{\mw{ो}}.

Then write \textbf{\mw{दो}}, \textbf{\mw{नो}}, \textbf{\mw{सो}} as a column, given out of order, and finish with \textbf{\mw{बीस}} and \textbf{\mw{दस} \mw{करो।}} from dictation. Repair only the missed sign and rewrite its word once.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
